events.text:
Dear Waypoint Mobility Forecasting Team,

I'm applying for the Data Scientist, Demand Forecasting role. Most of my work so far has been on the problem Waypoint works on: forecasting transit demand and getting planners to trust and use the forecasts.

As a research assistant in Lakeshore University's Urban Analytics Lab, I built bus ridership forecasting models in XGBoost and LightGBM. They used four years of automatic passenger counter data joined with anonymized third-party mobility data. I led the feature engineering and evaluation, and I'm first author of the resulting paper at the UrbanDS 2025 workshop. Compared with a SARIMA seasonal baseline, our model cut MAPE on a 2023 holdout from 14.2% to 9.8%. One reviewer was concerned that the mobility features might leak future information, so I re-ran the models with a longer lag. Accuracy was still well ahead of the baseline (10.4% MAPE), and the paper reports the stricter result. That process taught me that an evaluation setup has to hold up against the hardest question someone will ask, not just look good on the headline number.

Before graduate school, I spent a year as a data analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the Tableau and SQL ridership dashboards that the planning department used each week, and I automated our weekly reporting pipeline in Python, which cut prep time from about six hours to one. I also reworked dashboards so board members could read them. That job showed me how planners actually use numbers, and how fast trust goes when a forecast is presented with more certainty than it has.

This summer, as a data science intern at Northpoint Insurance, I built a gradient-boosted churn model that raised validation AUC from 0.71 to 0.76 over the logistic regression baseline. I calibrated its probabilities so the scores could be used as real likelihoods. I presented the results to the retention team and a VP, explaining what the model's metrics meant and which customer segments it flagged. The model was handed off for further evaluation. I haven't yet owned a model all the way into production, and I'd like to learn that by working with Waypoint's engineers.

I finish my M.S. in Data Science at Lakeshore in December 2026. I'd welcome the chance to bring my transit forecasting experience to the Forecasting team.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,
Morgan Reyes

---

I wrote this differently from the HealthBridge letter in a few places, so please check these:
- **Not "peer-reviewed":** I called the paper a workshop paper and didn't use "peer-reviewed," since it's non-archival.
- **Exact numbers:** I gave the actual MAPE figures instead of "over 30%." I also didn't mention a "prioritization strategy" at Northpoint, because the model was handed off rather than deployed.
- **Production gap:** I said openly that you haven't deployed a model yet, since the job description lists deployment as a bonus.
- **No PhD:** The PhD application isn't mentioned.
- **Name to fill in:** It's addressed to the team, so swap in the hiring manager's name if you find it.

Biography

Tianshi Li is an assistant professor in the Khoury College of Computer Sciences at Northeastern University, based in Boston.

After obtaining her doctorate in human–computer interaction, Li joined UC Berkeley as a postdoctoral scholar, where she continued her research on usable privacy and security in mobile apps and explored novel privacy issues in human–LLM interactions. Li also worked at Google, where she applied her techniques to products that provide privacy compliance support to companies. Specifically, she developed a series of integrated development environment plugins to assist developers in building mobile apps with native privacy support by adding privacy annotations to their source code. Li is particularly interested in enabling developers who don’t specialize in privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness to create apps that still meet privacy, security, accessibility, and fairness requirements. She has published work at the CHI, IMWUT/UbiComp, CSCW, and PETS conferences, as well as the TOCHI journal, and has earned several “best paper” honors.

Li was drawn to Khoury College by the opportunity to pursue rich collaborative research in cybersecurity, privacy, and HCI. She is dedicated to developing practical techniques in that leverage technological advancements to address pressing societal issues. She also hopes to direct her own lab.

When she isn’t working, Li enjoys playing board games and the guitar.

events.text:
**Statement of Purpose — Morgan Reyes, PhD in Computer Science (HCI), Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

In my Human-Centered Data Science course last spring, my team watched five classmates build models in an AutoML tool while they talked through what they were doing. All five took the top-ranked model without looking at its metrics. None of them opened the feature-importance panel. Two said they assumed the tool "knew" which columns were sensitive and would handle them. These were data science students, the kind of people the tool was made for. It was a small class project, but it changed which questions I care about. Most of my training has been in building models. I want to spend the next five years studying what happens between a model and the people who rely on it: what they think it knows, when they trust it, and what they believe they agreed to when their data went into it.

My path here runs through applied data science. After a B.A. in economics, I worked for a year as a data analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the ridership dashboards that our planning department used each week, and I automated our weekly reporting pipeline. The part of the job I remember most was not technical. A dashboard that worked fine for analysts confused board members, and I spent a lot of time reworking it until they could read it the way it was meant to be read. I saw that the same number can mean very different things to different audiences. I also saw that people stop trusting a forecast quickly once it has been presented with more confidence than it deserved.

As a research assistant in Prof. S. Patel's Urban Analytics Lab, I led feature engineering and evaluation for a bus ridership forecasting project. The resulting paper, on which I'm first author, appeared at the UrbanDS 2025 workshop. In review, one reviewer argued that our mobility features might leak future information. I re-ran the models with a longer lag. Accuracy dropped slightly but stayed well ahead of the seasonal baseline, and we reported the stricter result. That taught me to design evaluations around the hardest question a skeptic will ask. The project also left me with a question I couldn't answer from inside the model. Our mobility data came from apps whose users had given one-time opt-in consent. Reading the vendor's documentation, I doubted that the people who tapped "allow" had pictured their movements ending up in a transit agency's ridership model. The data was anonymized and aggregated, and the project followed the rules. Even so, I came away wanting to understand the gap between what consent technically covers and what people believe they have agreed to.

This past summer, as a data science intern at Northpoint Insurance, I built a churn model and presented it to the retention team and a VP. Most of my preparation went into explaining AUC and calibrated probabilities to people who would act on the model's scores without seeing how it worked. As a TA for STAT 1100, a statistics course for non-majors, I graded final data projects and wrote a rubric that included examples of strong and weak interpretation. Both jobs showed me how much of a model's effect depends on how people interpret it, which is the part data science training covers least.

These experiences point toward a set of research questions in human-AI interaction:

- **Reliance and overtrust:** How do people decide whether to rely on automated or AI-generated models? What interface designs help them calibrate that trust instead of handing judgment over to the tool?
- **Communicating uncertainty:** How should a forecast's uncertainty be shown to decision-makers, such as planners or managers, who don't have statistical training?
- **Consent and data use:** What do people believe happens to data they share through apps, and how could consent be designed so that it matches the uses their data actually goes to?

I don't yet know which of these will become my dissertation, and I expect my advisor and the first years of coursework to shape that. I do know I want to study these questions with people: through interviews, think-aloud and lab studies, and field work with real decision-makers. I also want to build and test interventions, not only describe problems. My modeling background should help here. I can build the systems I study, run realistic analyses on real data, and recognize when a user's mistaken belief about a model is actually a reasonable reading of a confusing interface.

[Faculty fit paragraph: name 1–3 Khoury faculty and connect a specific paper or project of theirs to one of the questions above.]

Khoury's HCI group fits the kind of researcher I want to become. It treats people, AI, and data practices as connected problems. I would bring practical experience with messy public-sector and industry data, the habit of putting results in front of non-technical audiences, and the motivation of someone who has seen these problems firsthand.

---

Some things to decide before you use this:

- **The consent paragraph uses a private remark of yours.** It's your comment that you doubted anyone tapping "allow" pictured this use. I left out the home-area feature that placed riders on specific blocks, because it suggests a re-identification risk in your lab's project, and Prof. Patel is writing one of your letters. Even without that, check that you're comfortable discussing the consent point. If not, I can cut it and build the statement around the reliance and uncertainty questions.
- **The faculty paragraph is a placeholder.** I did one quick web search. It turned up Tianshi Li, whose Khoury lab (PEACH) works on HCI, AI, and privacy. Their recent work includes human oversight of AI agents and usable privacy in mobile apps, which matches your consent question. That's one lead, not a full survey of the faculty. Look through Khoury's HCI faculty pages and pick the people you actually want to work with.
- **Wording stays close to the facts:** The usability study is described as a five-person class project, and the paper as a workshop paper. I also didn't present forecasting as your passion, since you told Prof. Patel you weren't sure you wanted another forecasting project.
- **Things to check against Khoury's instructions:** I titled this a statement of purpose. Check their required title, page or word limit, and whether they want separate research and personal statements.

**Statement of Purpose — Morgan Reyes, PhD in Computer Science (HCI), Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

As a research assistant, I spent most of a year building bus ridership forecasts from transit counts and third-party mobility data. One afternoon I read the vendor's documentation to find out how that mobility data was collected. It came from software built into partner apps, and users had given one-time opt-in consent. The data reached us anonymized and aggregated, and our project followed the rules. Still, I doubted that anyone who tapped "allow" had pictured their movements ending up in a transit agency's ridership model. I've kept coming back to that gap between what consent technically covers and what people believe they have agreed to. It's the question I want to spend a PhD on.

I came to this question through applied data science. After a B.A. in economics, I worked for a year as a data analyst at Lakeshore Regional Transit Authority. I maintained the ridership dashboards our planning department used each week and automated our weekly reporting pipeline. The part I remember most was not technical. A dashboard that worked fine for analysts confused board members, and I spent a lot of time reworking it until they read it the way it was meant to be read. That job showed me that the same information can mean very different things to different people, depending on how it's presented.

In Prof. S. Patel's Urban Analytics Lab, I led feature engineering and evaluation for the forecasting project. The resulting paper, on which I'm first author, appeared at the UrbanDS 2025 workshop. In review, one reviewer argued that our mobility features might leak future information. I re-ran the models with a longer lag, accuracy dropped slightly but stayed well ahead of the seasonal baseline, and we reported the stricter result. That taught me to design evaluations around the hardest question a skeptic will ask. It was also on this project that I read the vendor documentation and started asking the consent question. From inside the model, I had no way to answer it.

Last spring, a course project gave me my first chance to study a question like this with people. In Human-Centered Data Science, my team ran think-aloud sessions with five classmates using an AutoML tool. All five accepted the top-ranked model without checking its metrics, and none opened the feature-importance panel. The finding that stayed with me was that two participants assumed the tool "knew" which columns were sensitive and would handle them on its own. These were data science students, the people the tool was designed for. Yet they held confident, wrong beliefs about what the system was doing with their data. It was a small class project, but it suggested that the gap I'd noticed as an RA isn't only a problem for ordinary app users. It appears wherever people hand data to a system they can't see inside.

My other work has been about closing that kind of gap through explanation. As a data science intern at Northpoint Insurance this summer, I built a churn model and presented it to the retention team and a VP. Most of my preparation went into explaining AUC and calibrated probabilities to people who would act on the model's scores without seeing how it worked. As a TA for STAT 1100, a statistics course for non-majors, I wrote a grading rubric with examples of strong and weak interpretation. Both jobs taught me how much effort it takes to give someone an accurate picture of what a data system does, and how easily that picture goes wrong.

My central research question is **how people understand what happens to their data once they share it, and how consent and data-use interfaces could be designed so that what people agree to matches what is actually done with their data.** I'm interested in the gap between technically valid consent and informed consent, especially when data travels from one context into another, like app location data ending up in public-sector planning models. Two related questions support this one:

- **Beliefs about what systems know and do.** People form mental models of data systems, like my classmates who assumed the AutoML tool handled sensitive columns for them. How do those beliefs form, when are they wrong, and how do wrong beliefs shape what people are willing to share and rely on? Understanding these mental models seems like a prerequisite for designing consent that works.
- **Making data use understandable.** My forecasting and analytics work was largely about communicating complex, uncertain results to people without technical training. I want to apply that to consent: how can a system show downstream uses, aggregation, and risk in a form people actually understand, rather than a one-time "allow" button?

I don't yet know exactly what my dissertation will be, and I expect my advisor and early coursework to shape it. I do know I want to study these questions with people: through interviews, think-aloud and lab studies, and fieldwork. I also want to design and test alternatives, not only document problems. My modeling background should help here. I know from experience how mobility and behavioral data is joined, engineered, and modeled after collection. That lets me trace realistic paths from a consent screen to downstream uses, and build working prototypes to test.

[Faculty fit paragraph: name 1–3 Khoury faculty and connect a specific paper or project of theirs to the consent question or one of the two supporting questions.]

Khoury's HCI group fits the kind of researcher I want to become. It treats privacy, people, and AI as connected problems. I would bring firsthand experience with how data is used after collection in public-sector and industry settings, the habit of putting results in front of non-technical audiences, and a question I've been carrying since that afternoon with the vendor documentation.

I think the draft read like a cover letter because it was built like one. It went through your jobs one by one, quoted results, retold the reviewer story, and ended with "what I would bring." Here's a rewrite that spends most of its space on the questions and less on your résumé:

---

**Statement of Purpose — Morgan Reyes, PhD in Computer Science (HCI), Khoury College of Computer Sciences**

For most of 2025, I worked as a research assistant on a project forecasting bus ridership. Part of our data came from a vendor that collected location data through software built into partner apps. Partway through, I read the vendor's documentation to find out where the data came from. People had agreed to share their location once, by tapping "allow" in some app. Everything we did was anonymized, aggregated, and within the rules. My honest reaction was: I doubt anyone tapping "allow" pictured this.

I couldn't stop thinking about that. Technically, those people had consented. But I wasn't sure what they had actually agreed to, or whether anyone had ever asked them. And nothing in my training as a data scientist helped me answer it. I knew how to join their data to ridership counts, build features from it, and measure how much it improved a forecast. I had no way to find out what it meant to them.

When the paper came out, I mostly felt relieved. My advisor suggested a follow-up extending the model to light rail, and I realized I didn't want another forecasting project. What I wanted to study was the people on the other side of the data.

The first time I got to do that was a course project in Human-Centered Data Science. My team watched five classmates use an AutoML tool and asked them to think aloud. Two of them assumed the tool "knew" which columns in their data were sensitive and would handle them. It didn't. These were data science students, and they were confidently wrong about what a system was doing with their data, in the same way I suspected the app users were. It was a small study, and the first one I had ever run. But sitting with people while they worked taught me more than a year of modeling had, and it's the kind of work I want to keep doing.

Looking back, my earlier jobs pointed in this direction too. As a data analyst at a regional transit agency, I made dashboards. The work I remember is reworking one so board members could read it the way analysts did. As a TA for a statistics course for non-majors, I spent much of my time on how students interpreted results, not on how they calculated them. Both times, the hard part was the gap between what the data said and what people understood.

That gap is what I want to study. My central question is **what people believe happens to their data once they share it, and how consent could be designed so that what people agree to matches what is actually done with their data.** I'm most interested in data that moves out of the setting where it was collected, like location data from an app ending up in a transit agency's planning model. That movement is invisible to the person who shared the data, and a one-time "allow" can't describe it.

Two related questions feed into this one. First, how do people form their beliefs about what a data system knows and does? My classmates' assumptions about the AutoML tool weren't random. They came from somewhere, and consent can't be designed well without understanding them. Second, can the movement of data be made visible? Could people see where their data goes, how it's combined, and what it's used for, in a way they actually understand and that changes the choices they make?

I don't know yet exactly what my dissertation will be, and I want a PhD in part to find out with an advisor's help. I do know I want to answer these questions by talking to and watching people: interviews, think-aloud studies, and fieldwork. I also want to design and test alternatives to the "allow" button, not only document what's wrong with it. Having been the person on the receiving end of this data probably helps. I've seen what happens to it after people agree.

[Faculty fit paragraph: name 1–3 Khoury faculty and say what in their work you want to build on.]

I came to data science through economics because I wanted to understand how people make decisions. I've spent the last few years on the data instead. I'm applying to Khoury to get back to the people.

---

Two caveats:

1. **This isn't your voice yet.** I haven't seen much of your own writing. Mostly I've taken phrases you've said to me ("I doubt anyone tapping 'allow' pictured this," "something with people and AI, not just building models"). The fastest way to make it sound like you is to read it aloud and rewrite any sentence you wouldn't actually say.

Research

Position: LLM Privacy Requires a Lifecycle-Wide Approach

Niloofar Mireshghallah † , Tianshi Li †

NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track)

The discourse on privacy risks in Large Language Models (LLMs) has disproportionately focused on verbatim memorization of training data, while a constellation of more immediate and scalable privacy threats remain underexplored. This position paper argues that the privacy landscape of LLM systems extends far beyond training data extraction, encompassing risks from data collection practices, inference-time context leakage, autonomous agent capabilities, and the democratization of surveillance through deep inference attacks. We present a comprehensive taxonomy of privacy risks across the LLM lifecycle -- from data collection through deployment -- and demonstrate through case studies how current privacy frameworks fail to address these multifaceted threats. Through a longitudinal analysis of 1,322 AI/ML privacy papers published at leading conferences over the past decade (2016--2025), we reveal that while memorization receives outsized attention in technical research, the most pressing privacy harms lie elsewhere, where current technical approaches offer little traction and viable paths forward remain unclear. We call for a fundamental shift in how the research community approaches LLM privacy, moving beyond the narrow focus of current technical solutions and embracing interdisciplinary approaches that address the sociotechnical nature of these emerging threats.

arXiv

Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment

Zhiping Zhang, Franklin Mingzhe Li, Raio Zihao Huang, Tianshi Li

Preprint

When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. Each task is specified by an authorization contract that separates the principal's instruction, completion criteria, and out-of-authorization actions. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged (19.3% at low effort versus 19.1% at high effort), with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p = 0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment, motivating it as a distinct target for agent evaluation and development. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p

-->

AgentDoxx: Agentic Re-identification of Anonymized Text with Web Search

Jianing Wen, Tianshi Li

Preprint

As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain tool use capabilities such as web search, they can retrieve and cross-reference public information, creating privacy risks beyond memorization. One manifestation is re-identification: linking an anonymized interview transcript to a named individual. Yet without ground-truth identities, the coverage of such attacks and the protection offered by a defense cannot be reliably measured. We introduce AgentDoxx, an evaluation suite of 822 synthetic interview transcripts grounded in public information about real individuals with known identities. We evaluate fifteen configurations of open-weight and proprietary models, isolating the effect of web search, and analyze their search trajectories to distinguish retrieval-driven from parametric identifications. Ground-truth identities reveal that re-identification risk is distributed across an agent's execution: retrieval and parametric recall both contribute, with open-weight models identifying 15-28% of transcripts without search; identification succeeds in over 88% of cases once the target appears in a retrieved result; entity masking leaves at least one attacker successful on 85.3% of a stratified sample; and privacy instructions suppress naming but not retrieval, with configurations scoring 0% accuracy yet retrieving the subject in up to 62% of transcripts. We further show that observed attack trajectories can provide supervision for localizing identifying spans, offering a path toward attack-informed anonymization.

arXiv

-->

Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents

Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, Tianshi Li

COLM 2026

LLM agents require personal information for personalization in order to effectively act on users' behalf, but this raises privacy concerns that can discourage data sharing, limiting both the autonomy levels at which agents can operate and the effectiveness of personalization. Yet the expanded design space of agent autonomy also presents opportunities to shape these effects, which remain underexplored. We conducted a 3×3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) to study how agent autonomy level influences personalization's effects on users' privacy concerns, trust, and willingness to use, as well as the underlying psychological processes. We find that risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent delegates control back to users upon detecting potential privacy leakage, improves users' perceived control. This in turn attenuates personalization's adverse effects: privacy concerns rise less and trust declines less. Our results suggest that designing agent's autonomy that supports human autonomy (both perceived control and oversight effectiveness) helps users benefit from personalization without being deterred by growing privacy concerns. This positions aligning decision authority between users and agents (autonomy alignment) as an important opportunity and challenge for trustworthy human-agent interaction.
